results.result: Adiponectin is expressed by all bone marrow adipocytes (BMAds) and a subset of stromal progenitor cells in healthy mice. Lineage tracing using AdipoqCre+/mTmG+ mice showed GFP expression in all PLIN1+ rBMAT and cBMAT adipocytes, as well as in reticular stromal cells and bone lining cells. CFU assays revealed that 79.8±9.0% of colonies were completely adiponectin-positive, 16.5±9.1% were negative, and 3.7±0.3% were mixed, with spontaneous adipogenesis occurring only in GFP+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C32 provide converging evidence from in vivo lineage tracing (immunostaining) and in vitro CFU assays demonstrating that adiponectin is expressed by BMAds and their progenitors in healthy conditions. The quantitative data from multiple experimental approaches (n=3 mice, 166 colonies) with appropriate controls support the conclusion. The observation of transitional GFP+ granules in RFP+ cells (C29) provides additional mechanistic insight into adiponectin activation during progenitor maturation.

results.result: Fat-free (FF) mice lacking adiponectin-expressing cells exhibit complete loss of white and brown adipose tissues with secondary metabolic complications. FF mice at 4 and 8 months showed absence of peripheral fat and circulating adiponectin, accompanied by liver enlargement, hepatic steatosis, elevated blood glucose, and reduced tibia length (3-7%). Body mass changes were sex-dependent: males resisted age-associated weight gain while females were 9-13% heavier than controls at both ages.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are well-supported by multiple complementary measurements including western blot (adiponectin), histology (tissue architecture), glucometry, and morphometry across both sexes and two time points. The data demonstrate successful generation of the lipodystrophic phenotype with expected secondary metabolic consequences. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3-8 per group) with appropriate statistical testing (two-way ANOVA).

results.result: Ablation of adiponectin-expressing cells produces sex- and age-dependent effects on trabecular bone. Female FF mice showed sustained increases in trabecular bone volume fraction, number, thickness, and BMD with decreased spacing at both 4 and 8 months. Male FF mice exhibited less prominent increases at 4 months that normalized by 8 months, with decreased trabecular thickness at 8 months compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by comprehensive µCT analysis with appropriate quantification of multiple trabecular parameters. The sex-specific differences are clearly documented with statistical support (two-way ANOVA, n=3-8 per group). The conclusion (C47) appropriately reflects the differential responses between sexes. The data align with cited prior work (Zou et al., 2019) providing external validation.

results.result: Cortical bone changes in FF mice show early increases followed by age-related decline. At 4 months, both sexes showed increased cortical BVF and thickness, with decreased medullary area. However, from 4 to 8 months, both male and female FF mice exhibited significant decreases in cortical thickness (-19.0% and -19.1%, respectively), contrasting with controls where thickness remained constant (males) or increased by +16% (females).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by detailed µCT analysis of cortical bone parameters at multiple sites and time points. The longitudinal comparison reveals an important temporal pattern: early gains are not sustained and reverse with age. The contrast with control mice strengthens the interpretation. Statistical support is appropriate (two-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: BMAT persists in FF mice despite adiponectin-expressing cell ablation, but with ectopic localization and age-dependent expansion. Unlike controls where BMAT concentrated in proximal and distal tibia, FF mice showed BMAT predominantly in the proximal tibia and mid-diaphysis with minimal distal BMAT. Proximal tibial BMAT increased 6.9-fold (males) and 23.2-fold (females) with age in FF mice, compared to 2.2-fold and 5.6-fold in controls. BMAT was absent in FF tail vertebrae, a region of dense cBMAT in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C64 are strongly supported by osmium µCT imaging and quantification, providing both 3D visualization and regional volumetric analysis. The ectopic localization pattern is clearly documented and contrasts with established BMAT distribution patterns (cited: Scheller et al., 2015). The dramatic age-related expansion in FF mice (especially females) is well-quantified with appropriate statistics. The absence of BMAT in tail vertebrae (C63) provides important negative control data confirming selective depletion of cBMAT-like adipocytes.

results.result: FF bone marrow adipocytes are morphologically similar to control BMAds but larger in size, while peripheral adipocytes are replaced by macrophages. FF BMAds contained large central PLIN1+ lipid droplets and were CD68-negative, whereas infrapatellar adipocytes in FF mice were replaced by foam-cell-like, auto-fluorescent, PLIN1-, CD68+ macrophages. FF BMAT adipocytes were 13.7% (males) and 42.9% (females) larger than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by histological and immunostaining evidence clearly distinguishing bone marrow from peripheral adipocyte fates. The morphological characterization using PLIN1 and CD68 markers appropriately identifies adipocytes versus macrophages. Quantitative size analysis (C70) used appropriate methodology (>100 adipocytes per mouse) with statistical support. The contrast between bone marrow preservation and peripheral replacement strengthens the conclusion of selective BMAT retention.

results.result: FF mice show differential responses to cold stress compared to controls. At 22°C versus 30°C, trabecular BVF decreased 33-57% in both genotypes, but cortical thickness decreased 9-13% only in controls. Proximal tibial BMAT decreased 82% in controls but remained unchanged in FF mice. Unexpectedly, distal tibial BMAT increased 1.5-fold (controls) and 5-fold (FF) at 22°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by comprehensive µCT analysis of bone and osmium µCT of BMAT under two temperature conditions. The differential responses between genotypes are clearly documented with appropriate statistics (two-way ANOVA, n=4-5 per group). The unexpected increase in distal BMAT (C75) is appropriately noted and quantified. The conclusions (C76-C77) accurately summarize the genotype-specific responses, though the mechanism underlying the distal BMAT increase remains unexplained.

results.result: FF bone marrow adipocytes are resistant to β3-adrenergic stimulation and have decreased expression of lipolytic genes. CL316,243 treatment increased circulating glycerol 2.2-2.3-fold in controls but not in FF mice. β3-AR stimulation decreased BMAd size by 26% in controls but had no effect in FF mice. Gene expression analysis showed decreased Adrb3 and Mgll in FF BMAds, while Adrb2, Pnpla2, and Lipe were comparable to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85 are well-supported by functional studies (serum glycerol response), morphometric analysis (adipocyte size), and molecular data (qPCR). The chronic CL316,243 treatment protocol is clearly described with appropriate controls and time points. The selective decrease in Adrb3 and Mgll (C82) provides mechanistic insight into the functional resistance. Sample sizes for gene expression are limited (n=2 per group from pooled samples) but the functional data (n=4-6 per group) provide strong support for the resistance phenotype.

results.result: Subcutaneous fat transplantation rescues metabolic abnormalities and prevents ectopic BMAT expansion in FF mice. Fat transplant normalized body mass in FF females, corrected hyperglycemia in both sexes, and significantly reduced liver enlargement and hypertriglyceridemia. Transplanted adipose tissue mass was higher in FF mice than controls. Importantly, fat transplant prevented ectopic BMAT expansion in FF mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 are strongly supported by a well-designed intervention study with appropriate controls (sham surgery) and multiple outcome measures. The rescue of metabolic parameters (body mass, glucose, liver mass, triglycerides) is clearly documented with statistical support (two-way ANOVA, n=4-7 per group). The prevention of BMAT expansion (C90) is particularly important as it demonstrates the systemic metabolic contribution to ectopic BMAT formation. The 12-week duration provides adequate time for metabolic adaptation.

results.result: The majority of FF bone marrow adipocytes originate from adiponectin-negative progenitors. In triple-mutant FFmTmG mice, 41-56% of BMAds were RFP+ (adiponectin-negative), 6-21% were GFP+ (adiponectin-expressing), and ~38% had indeterminate membranes with both RFP and GFP. CFU assays showed 91% reduction in colony number, with spontaneous adipogenesis observed in both RFP+ and GFP+ progenitors in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by lineage tracing in triple-mutant mice combining DTA and mTmG reporters. The quantification of adipocyte membrane fluorescence (n=802 adipocytes from 6-7 bones) provides robust evidence for adiponectin-negative origins. The CFU data (C94-C95) confirm the dramatic depletion of adiponectin+ progenitors while demonstrating residual adipogenic capacity in adiponectin-negative cells. The presence of indeterminate cells (C93) suggests complexity in adiponectin expression dynamics, appropriately acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: FF bone marrow adipocytes show decreased expression of adiponectin and key cytokines but maintain expression of some adipogenic markers. Gene expression analysis revealed decreased Adipoq, Cxcl12, Cfd, Retn, and Pparg in FF BMAds, while Cebpa, Cd36, and Alpl were comparable to controls. Diphthamide biosynthesis genes (Dph1-7) showed no significant regulation, suggesting DTA resistance is not due to Dph deficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 are supported by qPCR analysis of purified BMAds with appropriate normalization to housekeeping genes and statistical testing (unpaired t-test with Holm-Sidak correction). The selective pattern of gene expression changes is clearly documented. However, the sample size is limited (n=2 per group from pooled samples representing 20-37 mice), which reduces confidence in the magnitude of changes. The negative result for Dph genes (C101) appropriately rules out one mechanism of DTA resistance but doesn't explain the survival of adiponectin+ cells observed in C92-C93.

results.result: The early high bone mass phenotype in FF mice is independent of peripheral fat loss and ectopic BMAT formation. Fat transplant normalized metabolic parameters and prevented BMAT expansion but did not alter the onset of increased trabecular bone, suggesting that bone changes are driven by local depletion of adiponectin-expressing cells in the skeleton.
results.evaluation: Claims C132 and C137 are supported by the fat transplant experiment showing dissociation between metabolic rescue and bone phenotype. The interpretation is strengthened by citation to prior work (Zhong et al., 2020) showing similar findings. However, the bone analysis in the transplant experiment is limited to basic parameters and lacks the temporal detail of the main aging study. The conclusion of independence is reasonable but could be strengthened by more comprehensive bone analysis in transplanted animals.

results.result: Depletion of adiponectin-expressing cells leads to suppression of cortical bone maintenance with age. Despite early increases, both male and female FF mice showed decreased cortical thickness from 4 to 8 months, suggesting that adiponectin-expressing progenitors (MALP/Adipo-CAR cells) may be necessary for maintaining bone integrity through recruitment to the osteoblast lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 are supported by the longitudinal µCT data showing age-related cortical bone decline in FF mice. The interpretation (C134) is appropriately cautious ('may provide necessary contributions') and is supported by citation to Matsushita et al., 2020 showing MALP recruitment to osteoblasts. However, the mechanism remains speculative as direct evidence for impaired osteoblast recruitment is not provided. The correlation between progenitor depletion and bone decline is clear, but causation is inferred rather than demonstrated.

results.result: The relationship between BMAT and bone differs between control and FF mice and between trabecular and cortical compartments. In controls, trabecular BVF was inversely correlated with metaphyseal BMAT (R²=0.137, p=0.037), but this association was absent in FF mice (R²=0.073, p=0.155). Conversely, diaphyseal BMAT was inversely correlated with cortical BVF in FF mice (R²=0.306, p=0.002) but not controls (R²=0.044, p=0.252).
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140, C142 are supported by correlation analysis across multiple experiments (n=29-32 mice per group). The statistical approach is appropriate for identifying associations. However, the R² values are relatively low (0.137-0.306), indicating that BMAT explains only a modest fraction of bone variance. The authors appropriately note they 'cannot presume causation' (C143). The differential correlations between genotypes and compartments are interesting but the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative. The sample size pooled across experiments may introduce heterogeneity.

results.result: FF bone marrow adipocytes share molecular features with aged BMAds, including decreased Cxcl12 and Adipoq expression. The 87% decrease in Cxcl12 in FF BMAds aligns with 46% decrease in aged BMAds (18 vs 6 months) and 24-41% decrease in obese mice. The authors propose that expansion of adiponectin-/lo, Cxcl12-/lo BMAds is a conserved adaptation with age and metabolic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 are supported by the gene expression data from FF BMAds and comparison to re-analyzed published microarray data (Liu et al., 2011, 2013). The parallel between FF and aged/obese BMAds is compelling. However, the proposal (C118) that this represents a 'conserved adaptation' is somewhat speculative as it extrapolates from the FF model to normal aging. The re-analysis of published data strengthens the argument but direct comparison of FF and aged mice in the same study would be more definitive. The sex-specific BMAT expansion pattern (C113) aligns with cited aging studies.

results.result: Rodent bone marrow adipocytes can undergo adaptations similar to aged human BMAds, including resistance to lipolysis due to decreased Mgll expression. The selective decrease in Mgll in FF BMAds parallels findings in aged human BMAds, while other lipases (ATGL, HSL) remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by comparison of the FF BMAd gene expression profile to published human data (Attané et al., 2020). The parallel decrease in Mgll between FF mice and aged humans is compelling. However, the conclusion (C124) that 'rodent BMAds can undergo the same adaptations' is somewhat overstated as the FF model involves genetic ablation rather than natural aging. The comparison is valuable but the mechanisms may differ. Additionally, FF mice show decreased Adrb3 while this was not reported in the human study, suggesting some differences in adaptation.

results.result: Adiponectin is expressed by a subset of bone marrow stromal progenitor cells that overlap with CAR cells/MALPs. These adiponectin-expressing progenitors are largely PDGFRβ+ and VCAM-1+, appear postnatally (P1+), and have gene expression patterns characteristic of pre-adipocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by the lineage tracing data presented in this study combined with extensive citations to recent single-cell RNAseq and lineage tracing studies (Matsushita et al., 2020; Baccin et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2020; Mukohira et al., 2019). The integration of the current findings with published literature is appropriate. However, these claims rely heavily on cited work rather than new data generated in this study. The postnatal appearance (C106) is inferred from cited studies rather than directly demonstrated here.

results.result: The location of adiponectin-/low FF BMAds aligns with arteriolar distribution, suggesting they may originate from Osteo-CAR cells. Depletion of peri-sinusoidal adiponectin+ MALP/Adipo-CAR progenitors drives preferential differentiation of adiponectin-/lo, Cxcl12-/lo progenitors into adipocytes in states of metabolic demand.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 propose a model for FF BMAd origins based on anatomical location and cited literature on progenitor populations. While the ectopic BMAT localization is well-documented (C107), the inference that these cells originate from Osteo-CAR cells is speculative and not directly tested. The model (C111) is logical and integrates published findings about MALP/Adipo-CAR and Osteo-CAR populations, but lacks direct lineage tracing or marker analysis to confirm the proposed cellular origins. The hypothesis is reasonable but requires additional experimental validation such as Osteo-CAR-specific lineage tracing or marker analysis of FF BMAds.

results.result: The secondary adipogenesis pathway is unique to bone marrow because peripheral adipose tissues lack alternate progenitor populations. This explains why FF mice completely lose peripheral fat while retaining bone marrow adipocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C145 propose that the bone marrow-specific retention of adipocytes in FF mice is due to the presence of alternate (adiponectin-negative) progenitors that don't exist in peripheral depots. While the observation of selective BMAT retention is well-documented, the explanation is speculative. The authors have not directly tested whether peripheral adipose depots contain adiponectin-negative progenitors capable of adipogenesis. The inference is reasonable based on the phenotype, but alternative explanations (e.g., differential DTA sensitivity, microenvironmental protection) are not fully excluded. Direct testing of adipogenic capacity of peripheral adiponectin-negative progenitors would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Decreased Cxcl12 expression in FF BMAds may impair hematopoietic support, and these cells may have limited endocrine and secretory functions due to decreased expression of multiple adipokines (Cxcl12, Adipoq, adipsin, resistin).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 propose functional consequences of the observed gene expression changes but lack direct functional validation. While the gene expression data clearly show decreased cytokine expression (C98), the actual impact on hematopoiesis or endocrine function is not tested. The speculation about hematopoietic support (C119) is supported by citation to Mattiucci et al., 2018 on Cxcl12 function, but no hematopoietic parameters are measured in FF mice. Similarly, the inference about 'limited endocrine and secretory functions' (C120) is reasonable but not directly demonstrated. Functional assays (e.g., hematopoietic colony assays, secretion studies) would be needed to support these claims.

results.result: Excess circulating lipids contribute to ectopic BMAT development, and normalization of lipid levels through fat transplantation can prevent BMAT expansion. This supports the paradigm that circulating lipids drive BMAT formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 are supported by the fat transplant experiment showing that metabolic normalization prevents BMAT expansion. The rescue of hypertriglyceridemia (C89) coincides with prevention of BMAT expansion (C90), supporting a causal relationship. However, the interpretation (C126-C127) involves some inference as multiple metabolic parameters are normalized simultaneously (glucose, triglycerides, liver function), making it difficult to isolate the specific contribution of circulating lipids. The conclusion aligns with 'existing paradigm' (C126) supported by general knowledge, but the mechanism could involve other factors beyond lipids alone.

results.result: Depletion of adiponectin-expressing cells limits bone elongation, potentially through effects on growth plate chondrocytes. FF mice showed 3-7% reduction in tibia length, and short stature is consistently reported in CGL3 patients whose BMAT is also preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 are supported by the tibia length measurements (C37) and citation to clinical literature on CGL3 (Kim et al., 2008). The observation of reduced bone length is clear and statistically significant. However, the proposed mechanism (C129) involving 'suppression of chondrocyte differentiation and/or proliferation' is speculative as no growth plate analysis is presented. The parallel to CGL3 patients (C130) strengthens the clinical relevance but doesn't establish mechanism. The claim would be better supported by histological analysis of the growth plate or chondrocyte markers.

results.result: AdipoqCre+/DTA+ FF mice have low levels of estradiol, which may contribute to sex-dependent bone phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 is supported by citation to Brenot et al., 2020. However, this is entirely based on prior published work and no estradiol measurements are presented in the current study. The relevance to the observed sex differences in bone phenotype is speculative. While low estradiol could explain some sex-specific effects, the authors don't directly test this hypothesis or measure estradiol levels in their cohorts. This represents an important confounding variable that should be acknowledged but is not experimentally addressed in this work.

results.result: The relationship between BMAT expansion and bone loss has been questioned in recent years, with multiple models showing high bone mass and high BMAT can occur simultaneously. BMAT expansion is not necessary for age-associated bone loss but may intensify cortical porosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 are supported by citations to recent literature (Scheller et al., 2015; Fazeli et al., 2013; Almeida et al., 2020) and align with the findings in FF mice showing early high bone mass with BMAT expansion. These claims represent a synthesis of published literature rather than new findings from this study. The citations are appropriate and the interpretation is consistent with current understanding in the field. However, these are primarily literature-based claims rather than results from the current experiments.

results.result: MALP cells form a peri-sinusoidal network and secrete RANKL to suppress trabecular bone, while ectopic adiponectin-/low BMAds may originate from Osteo-CAR cells near arterioles and affect cortical bone. This could explain the differential correlations between BMAT and bone compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C141 and C143 propose a model to explain the differential BMAT-bone correlations based on progenitor cell localization and function. While C141 is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2021 regarding MALP function, the hypothesis about Osteo-CAR origins (C143) is speculative. The authors appropriately state they 'cannot presume causation' and this is presented as a hypothesis. The model is logical and integrates published findings, but lacks direct experimental support such as lineage tracing from Osteo-CAR cells or demonstration of arteriolar localization of FF BMAds. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring future validation.

results.result: A unique population of BMAds specialized for lipid storage with limited lipid mobilization and endocrine functions accumulates with age and metabolic disease through a novel secondary adipogenesis pathway unique to bone marrow. The spatially defined progenitor cell, systemic metabolic profile, and local microenvironment are necessary regulators of BMAd expansion and adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C144, C146, and C147 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data on FF BMAd characteristics (increased size, decreased cytokine expression, resistance to lipolysis, adiponectin-negative origins) and the effects of metabolic manipulation (fat transplant) and environmental stress (cold exposure). The integration of progenitor identity, metabolic state, and microenvironment (C146) is supported by the experimental manipulations. However, the generalization to 'age and metabolic disease' (C144) extrapolates somewhat from the genetic model to natural conditions, though this is supported by comparison to aged BMAd gene expression profiles.

results.result: Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) accumulates with age and diverse disease states, acts as an endocrine organ and energy storage depot, and varies in development and regulation between skeletal sites. BMAT expansion occurs in conditions including anorexia, obesity, aging, osteoporosis, and various treatments, many associated with increased fracture risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C12 provide background context supported by citations to review articles and established literature (Scheller et al., 2016b, 2015, 2019; Craft et al., 2018; Fazeli et al., 2013). These represent well-established knowledge in the field rather than new findings from this study. The claims are appropriately cited and provide necessary context for understanding the significance of the work. The distinction between cBMAT and rBMAT (C9-C10) is well-established in prior literature.

results.result: Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (CGL) is characterized by complete loss of peripheral adipose tissues, but BMAT is selectively preserved in CGL3 (CAV1 mutations) and CGL4 (PTRF mutations) but not CGL1 or CGL2. Similarly, all BMAT is retained in Cav1 knockout mice and cBMAT is present in Ptrf knockouts.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 provide important background on lipodystrophy and BMAT preservation, supported by citations to clinical and mouse model literature (Scheller and Rosen, 2014a; Fiorenza et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2019; Teboul-Coré et al., 2016; Scheller et al., 2015). These establish the rationale for using the FF mouse model to study BMAT preservation mechanisms. The claims are well-supported by cited literature and provide essential context, though they represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: The fat-free mouse model is based on Adipoq-Cre-driven expression of diphtheria toxin A (DTA), which kills adiponectin-expressing cells. Adiponectin is expressed by all adipocytes in healthy mice and defines the major BMAd progenitor (Adipo-CAR/MALP cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 describe the genetic basis of the FF model and adiponectin expression patterns, supported by citations to the DTA system (Ivanova et al., 2005; Voehringer et al., 2008), adiponectin expression (Craft et al., 2019), and recent progenitor cell studies (Zhong et al., 2020; Matsushita et al., 2020; Baccin et al., 2020). These provide essential methodological context and are well-supported by cited literature. The description of the genetic system (C18) is accurate based on established Cre-lox and DTA mechanisms.

results.result: A novel secondary adipogenesis pathway in bone marrow relies on adiponectin-negative stromal progenitors, is unique to bone marrow, and is activated with age and metabolic stress. This pathway produces BMAds specialized for lipid storage with compromised lipid mobilization and cytokine expression in regions traditionally devoted to hematopoiesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C6 represent the central thesis of the paper, stated in the abstract. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including: lineage tracing showing adiponectin-negative origins (C92-C96), ectopic localization in hematopoietic regions (C54-C64), age-dependent expansion (C59-C60), increased adipocyte size (C70), resistance to lipolysis (C78-C85), and decreased cytokine expression (C97-C98). The claim of uniqueness to bone marrow (C3) is supported by complete peripheral fat loss (C33) versus BMAT retention (C54). The integration of all experimental findings strongly supports these summary claims.
